---
title: "Breaking a Continuous Symmetry — Goldstone's Theorem"
---

> [!TLDR]
> A complex scalar field with global U(1) symmetry has a circle of degenerate minima. Tangential fluctuations are massless Goldstone modes, while radial fluctuations are massive.

Consider a complex scalar field $\signal{\Phi}$ with Lagrangian density
$$
\energy{\mathcal{L}}
=(\partial_\mu\signal{\Phi}^*)(\partial^\mu\signal{\Phi})
-\energy{V}(\signal{\Phi}),
\qquad
\energy{V}(\signal{\Phi})
=-\energy{\mu}^2\lvert\signal{\Phi}\rvert^2
+\signal{\lambda}\lvert\signal{\Phi}\rvert^4,
$$
where $\energy{\mu}^2>0$ and $\signal{\lambda}>0$.
It is invariant under the global $U(1)$ transformation
$$
\signal{\Phi}\to e^{i\alpha}\signal{\Phi},
\qquad\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.
$$
The minima form a continuous manifold:
$$
\lvert\signal{\Phi}\rvert^2
=\frac{\energy{\mu}^2}{2\signal{\lambda}}
=\frac{\signal{v}^2}{2}.
$$
Thus, the vacua form a circle of radius $\signal{v}/\sqrt{2}$ in the complex plane
$(\operatorname{Re}\signal{\Phi},\operatorname{Im}\signal{\Phi})$.
The potential is called a **Mexican hat**, or **sombrero**, potential.

**Fig. 13.2** Mexican-hat potential V = −μ²|Φ|² + λ|Φ|⁴. The red circle is the manifold of minima. The blue tangent direction is associated with the massless Goldstone mode. The green radial direction is associated with the massive Higgs mode. Drag the 3D view to rotate it.

> [!note]
> The plot uses dimensionless horizontal coordinates $\sqrt{2}\operatorname{Re}\signal{\Phi}/\signal{v}$ and $\sqrt{2}\operatorname{Im}\signal{\Phi}/\signal{v}$. The vertical shape is shifted by a constant so that the minimum is zero. The colored arrows indicate tangent and radial directions at one chosen vacuum.

Choose the real positive vacuum
$\langle\signal{\Phi}\rangle=\signal{v}/\sqrt{2}$.
Write fluctuations in terms of two real fields, $\signal{h}(\mechanical{x})$ and $\signal{\theta}(\mechanical{x})$:
$$
\signal{\Phi}(\mechanical{x})
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\left(\signal{v}+\signal{h}(\mechanical{x})\right)
e^{i\signal{\theta}(\mechanical{x})/\signal{v}}.
\tag{13.1}
$$
Substitute into the Lagrangian density and expand to second order:
$$
\energy{\mathcal{L}}
=\frac{1}{2}(\partial_\mu\signal{h})^2
-\energy{\mu}^2\signal{h}^2
+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_\mu\signal{\theta})^2
+\text{interactions}.
$$
The radial field $\signal{h}$ has mass
$\mechanical{m}_h^2=2\energy{\mu}^2$ and is the Higgs mode.
The field $\signal{\theta}$ is massless and is the **Goldstone boson**.

> [!note]
> **Theorem 13.2: Goldstone (1961).** Let $G$ be a continuous symmetry group of the Lagrangian density, and let $H\subset G$ be the subgroup that leaves the vacuum invariant. Spontaneous breaking gives $\dim G-\dim H$ massless scalar Goldstone bosons.
>
> This counting applies to continuous internal global symmetries under the usual relativistic assumptions, including a Lorentz-invariant vacuum. It does not exclude additional massless particles for other reasons.

The distinction between the two fluctuations is geometric. Moving around the vacuum circle costs no potential energy; moving away from the circle changes its radius and costs potential energy. In the polar variables of (13.1), the phase enters the kinetic term only through derivatives. The factor of the vacuum parameter in the exponent gives the phase field a canonical quadratic kinetic term, so its vanishing potential curvature means zero mass at this order.

The argument below is a Hessian proof for the scalar potential with canonical kinetic terms. It identifies the flat directions of a stationary classical vacuum. Its application to exact quantum masses requires the global-symmetry and relativistic assumptions stated in Theorem 13.2. A local gauge transformation instead relates redundant descriptions; the gauge-field constraints change the physical state counting, as [[13.02 The Higgs Mechanism]] explains. Before using the theorem, identify whether the symmetry is global or local.

## Proof

Let $\energy{V}(\signal{\phi}_i)$ be the potential for real scalar fields $\{\signal{\phi}_i\}$, and let $T^a$, with $a=1,\ldots,\dim G$, be the group generators.
Invariance implies
$$
\energy{V}(\signal{\phi})
=\energy{V}\left(\signal{\phi}
+\varepsilon^a(T^a)_{ij}\signal{\phi}_j\right)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(T^a)_{ij}\signal{\phi}_j
\frac{\partial\energy{V}}{\partial\signal{\phi}_i}=0
\quad\text{for all }a.
$$
Differentiate with respect to $\signal{\phi}_k$ and evaluate at the minimum $\signal{\phi}_j=\signal{v}_j$.
The source writes
$$
\left.
(T^a)_{ij}\signal{v}_j
\frac{\partial^2\energy{V}}
{\partial\signal{\phi}_k\partial\signal{\phi}_i}
\right|_{\signal{\phi}=\signal{v}}
+
\left.
(T^a)_{kj}
\frac{\partial\energy{V}}{\partial\signal{\phi}_j}
\right|_{\signal{\phi}=\signal{v}}
=0.
$$
At the minimum,
$\left.\partial\energy{V}/\partial\signal{\phi}_j\right|_{\signal{v}}=0$.
Thus,
$$
\mechanical{\mathcal{M}}_{ki}^2(T^a)_{ij}\signal{v}_j=0,
\qquad
\mechanical{\mathcal{M}}_{ki}^2
\equiv
\left.
\frac{\partial^2\energy{V}}
{\partial\signal{\phi}_k\partial\signal{\phi}_i}
\right|_{\signal{\phi}=\signal{v}}.
$$

> [!note]
> In the source's differentiated identity, the second term has transposed generator indices. Direct differentiation gives $(T^a)_{ik}\,\partial\energy{V}/\partial\signal{\phi}_i$. That term vanishes at the stationary vacuum, so this index error does not change the displayed mass-matrix conclusion.

The Hessian $\mechanical{\mathcal{M}}^2$ is the mass-squared matrix.
For a generator $T^a$ that does not annihilate the vacuum,
$T^a\signal{v}\ne0$, the vector $T^a\signal{v}$ is a zero eigenvector of $\mechanical{\mathcal{M}}^2$.
The generators that annihilate $\signal{v}$ form the Lie algebra of the unbroken subgroup $H$.
The remaining $\dim G-\dim H$ independent broken directions give the massless Goldstone modes.

In the $U(1)$ example, $G=U(1)$ has dimension one and $H=\{e\}$ has dimension zero.
There is one Goldstone boson, the field $\signal{\theta}$.
This agrees with the circle $S^1$ of minima.

## Example 13.3: O(N)/O(N − 1) sigma model

Consider $N$ real scalar fields $\signal{\phi}_i$ with $O(N)$ symmetry and potential
$$
\energy{V}
=-\frac{\energy{\mu}^2}{2}\lvert\signal{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\rvert^2
+\frac{\signal{\lambda}}{4}\lvert\signal{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\rvert^4.
$$
Choose the vacuum direction
$$
\langle\signal{\phi}_i\rangle=\signal{v}\delta_{iN}.
$$
It leaves $O(N-1)$, which rotates the first $N-1$ components, unbroken.
The number of Goldstone bosons is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\dim O(N)-\dim O(N-1)
&=\frac{N(N-1)}{2}-\frac{(N-1)(N-2)}{2}\\
&=N-1.
\end{aligned}
$$
For $N=4$, the case relevant to the electroweak scalar sector, there are three Goldstone modes.

> [!note]
> The source calls this a nonlinear sigma model. The displayed quartic potential describes the linear scalar model with a radial mode. The nonlinear sigma model results when the radial magnitude is constrained or the heavy radial mode is integrated out.

## Physical quantities

| Symbol | Unit | Quantity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\signal{\Phi},\signal{\Phi}^*$ | $\unit{MeV}$ | Complex scalar field | The field and its conjugate in the global-symmetry model. |
| $\energy{\mathcal{L}},\energy{V}$ | $\unit{MeV^4}$ | Lagrangian and potential densities | The scalar dynamics and its symmetry-breaking potential. |
| $\energy{\mu}$ | $\unit{MeV}$ | Potential mass scale | The scale in the negative quadratic coefficient. |
| $\signal{\lambda}$ | $1$ | Quartic coupling | The positive interaction coefficient. |
| $\signal{v}$ | $\unit{MeV}$ | Vacuum magnitude parameter | The parameter for which the vacuum circle has radius v/√2. |
| $\signal{h},\signal{\theta}$ | $\unit{MeV}$ | Radial and Goldstone fields | The real fluctuations with canonical quadratic kinetic terms. |
| $\mechanical{x}$ | $\unit{MeV^{-1}}$ | Spacetime coordinate | The position of the fluctuating complex field. |
| $\mechanical{m}_h$ | $\unit{MeV}$ | Radial-mode mass | The positive mass from the potential curvature. |
| $\signal{\phi}_i,\signal{v}_i$ | $\unit{MeV}$ | Real scalar components and vacuum values | The fields and stationary vacuum in the general proof. |
| $\mechanical{\mathcal{M}}^2$ | $\unit{MeV^2}$ | Scalar mass-squared matrix | The Hessian of the potential at the vacuum. |
